modules.title: Commercial Banking and Credit Creation
modules.html:
Commercial (Deposit Money) Banks

Financial institutions that accept deposits, lend money and provide payment services for profit.

Accounts
AccountFeatures
CurrentCheque book, no/low interest, overdraft possible
SavingsSmall deposits, earns interest, withdrawal limits
Fixed/time depositFixed sum for a fixed period at high interest
DomiciliaryHeld in foreign currency
Functions
  1. Accepting deposits and safekeeping valuables.
  2. Lending: overdrafts, term loans, discounting bills.
  3. Agency services: standing orders, direct debits, share purchase, executorship.
  4. Foreign exchange, letters of credit, travellers' cheques.
  5. Advisory and cash-management services; issuing cards and e-banking.

Credit Creation

Banks lend most of the money deposited with them, and loans return to the system as fresh deposits. The maximum expansion is given by the credit (bank deposit) multiplier:

$$\text{Credit Multiplier} = \dfrac{1}{\text{Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)}}$$ $$\text{Total Deposits Created} = \text{Initial Deposit} \times \dfrac{1}{\text{CRR}}$$
Limitations on credit creation
  • Level of cash reserve ratio imposed by the CBN
  • Amount of initial/primary deposits
  • Willingness of the public to borrow and to hold cash
  • Availability of good collateral and monetary policy stance

examples.q: A bank receives an initial deposit of ₦2,000,000 and the cash reserve ratio is 20%. Find the credit multiplier and the total deposits that can be created.
If the CBN raises the CRR from 20% to 25%, what happens to the same ₦2,000,000 deposit?
examples.a: \( \text{Multiplier} = \dfrac{1}{0.25} = 4 \), so total deposits fall to \( 2{,}000{,}000 \times 4 = ₦8{,}000{,}000 \). Credit creation shrinks by ₦2,000,000 – this is how a higher CRR tightens money supply and fights inflation.

modules.title: The Central Bank of Nigeria and Monetary Policy
modules.html:
Functions of the CBN

  1. Issue of currency – sole right to print notes and mint coins.
  2. Banker to the government – keeps government accounts, manages public debt.
  3. Banker to other banks – holds their reserves and clears cheques.
  4. Lender of last resort – rescues solvent but illiquid banks.
  5. Custodian of external reserves and manager of the exchange rate.
  6. Regulation and supervision of banks and other financial institutions.
  7. Formulation of monetary policy and promotion of development finance.

Instruments of Monetary Policy

InstrumentHow it works
Open market operationsSale of securities mops up cash; purchase injects cash
Monetary policy rate (MPR)A higher benchmark rate raises the cost of borrowing
Cash reserve ratioHigher CRR reduces lendable funds and the multiplier
Liquidity ratioMinimum liquid assets banks must keep
Selective credit controlDirects credit to priority sectors
Moral suasion & special directivesPersuasion and administrative instruction

Other Institutions

  • Merchant/investment banks – wholesale banking, equipment leasing, issuing houses.
  • Development banks – BOI, BOA, NEXIM, Development Bank of Nigeria.
  • NDIC – insures bank deposits.
  • Microfinance banks, mortgage banks, finance houses, bureaux de change, PFAs.
  • Fintech and mobile money operators – agency banking, payment gateways, USSD transfers.

examples.q: Inflation is rising sharply. Recommend three CBN actions and explain how each works.
examples.a: (1) Raise the MPR – loans become dearer, borrowing and spending fall. (2) Sell treasury bills through open market operations – cash is withdrawn from the banking system. (3) Increase the cash reserve ratio – banks keep more idle cash, the credit multiplier \( \frac{1}{CRR} \) falls and money supply contracts.

examples.q: Distinguish between the CBN and a commercial bank in three ways.
examples.a: Ownership: government-owned vs mainly private shareholders. Motive: monetary stability and regulation vs profit. Customers: government and banks vs the general public. Only the CBN issues currency and acts as lender of last resort.

modules.title: The Capital Market and the Stock Exchange
modules.html:
Money Market vs Capital Market

BasisMoney marketCapital market
PeriodShort term (under 1 year)Medium and long term
InstrumentsTreasury bills, call money, certificates of deposit, commercial papers, bills of exchangeShares, debentures, bonds, mortgages
InstitutionsCBN, commercial & merchant banks, discount housesNGX, SEC, issuing houses, stockbrokers, unit trusts

The Nigerian Exchange (NGX)

A market where existing securities are bought and sold. It has a primary market (new issues – offer for subscription, offer for sale, rights issue, private placement) and a secondary market (trading in existing securities).

Functions
  1. Provides long-term capital for companies and government.
  2. Gives liquidity – investors can convert shares into cash.
  3. Values securities and publishes prices; the All-Share Index measures market performance.
  4. Encourages savings and wider share ownership.
  5. Serves as a barometer of the economy.
Operators
  • Stockbroker – buys and sells on behalf of clients for commission.
  • Jobber/dealer – deals in securities on own account.
  • Issuing house – arranges new issues.
  • Registrar – keeps the register of members and pays dividends.
  • SEC – apex regulator of the capital market.

Useful Formulae

$$\text{Dividend Yield} = \dfrac{\text{Dividend per Share}}{\text{Market Price per Share}} \times 100$$ $$\text{Earnings per Share} = \dfrac{\text{Profit after Tax} - \text{Preference Dividend}}{\text{Number of Ordinary Shares}}$$

examples.q: A company pays a dividend of ₦1.20 per share; the market price is ₦15.00. Compute the dividend yield and interpret it.
examples.a: \( \text{Dividend Yield} = \dfrac{1.20}{15.00}\times100 = 8\% \). An investor buying at ₦15 earns an 8% cash return on the market value, which can be compared with bank interest or treasury-bill rates.

examples.q: Profit after tax is ₦48,000,000, preference dividend ₦8,000,000 and there are 20,000,000 ordinary shares. Find EPS.
examples.a: \( \text{EPS} = \dfrac{48{,}000{,}000 - 8{,}000{,}000}{20{,}000{,}000} = ₦2.00 \) per share – the earnings attributable to each ordinary share, whether distributed or retained.
